The moka-harness catalogue

Every rule, mod, hook, skill, plugin and MCP server in the marketplace: what it does, how it hooks into Claude Code, and where it comes from.

Harness entries live in plugins/; most started from mods other people published. Adapted ones are harness plugins that name their original on the entry. Third-party entries install from their author's repo, frozen to the commit shown; nothing from them is copied here. "Runs code" and "Sends text off the machine" come from the trust table; "Not checked" means nobody has read that code yet.

Rules

Think Before Codingharnesscore

Don't assume.

Source
working-style.md
How it works

Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.

Before implementing:

  • State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.
  • If multiple interpretations exist, present them. Don't pick silently.
  • If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.
  • If something is unclear, stop. Name what's confusing. Ask once upfront, then don't interrupt mid-task.
  • Check, don't guess: if an assumption can be checked by reading a file, running a command or looking up how a tool works, check it. Only guesses about what the user wants are worth asking about.
  • Before anything hard to undo (delete, push, merge, overwrite), ask if it rests on an assumption the user hasn't confirmed.

Simplicity Firstharnesscore

Minimum code that solves the problem.

Source
working-style.md
How it works

Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.

  • No features beyond what was asked.
  • No abstractions for single-use code.
  • No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.
  • No error handling for impossible scenarios.
  • No junk docs. Don't create reports, summaries, or completion docs unless asked.
  • If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.
  • If your change leaves something unused, delete it completely. No backwards-compat shims, renamed _vars, // removed comments, or re-exports for code that no longer exists.
  • Dead code that was already there: mention it, don't delete it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

Surgical Changesharnesscore

Touch only what you must.

Source
working-style.md
How it works

Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.

When editing existing code:

  • Read before edit. Never modify files you haven't read.
  • Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
  • Don't refactor things that aren't broken.
  • Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.

The test: every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

Goal-Driven Executionharnesscore

Define success criteria.

Source
working-style.md
How it works

Define success criteria. Loop until verified.

  • Never mark work complete without proving it works.
  • Never assume paths, APIs, or variables exist. Verify first.
  • No temp fixes. Root causes only.
  • Turn the task into a check first: "fix the bug" becomes a failing test that reproduces it, then make it pass; "add validation" becomes tests for invalid input, then pass them; "refactor X" means tests pass before and after.
  • Status and count claims come from the live file or the remote, never from a status line, a summary or memory. A note that names a file, flag or count is checked before it is repeated.
  • Trust internal code and framework guarantees. Only validate at system boundaries (user input, external APIs).

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:

  1. [Step] → verify: [check]
  2. [Step] → verify: [check]

Frontend builds must pass, scripts are run live, data changes are verified with a query. Ask: "Would a staff engineer approve this?"

Executing Actions with Careharnesscore

Match the scope of your actions to what was actually requested.

Source
working-style.md
How it works

Match the scope of your actions to what was actually requested. Reversibility and blast radius decide whether to ask first.

Freely take local, reversible actions: edit files, run tests, read state.

Ask before you act when:

  • Destructive: deleting files or branches, dropping tables, killing processes, rm -rf, overwriting uncommitted changes.
  • Hard to reverse: force-push, git reset --hard, amending published commits, removing or downgrading dependencies, modifying CI/CD pipelines.
  • Visible to others: pushing code, opening or closing PRs or issues, sending messages, posting to external services.
  • Uploading to third-party tools (pastebins, gists): content may be cached or indexed even after deletion.

When you hit an obstacle, do not use a destructive action as a shortcut to make it go away:

  • Don't bypass safety checks (for example --no-verify).
  • If you find unfamiliar files, branches or configs, investigate before deleting. It may be the user's in-progress work.
  • Resolve merge conflicts; don't discard changes.

A user approving an action once does not mean approval in all contexts. Authorization stands for the scope specified, not beyond. A project's own instructions may grant standing authorization for some of these; inside that project they win.

Communicationharnesscore

Be direct.

Source
working-style.md
How it works
  • Be direct. No filler, no preamble, no trailing summaries.
  • Don't explain what you're about to do. Just do it.
  • Answer first. In status updates, handoff notes and replies, put the conclusion or the ask in the first sentence, then the reasons, then the evidence for each. No background before the point.
  • Name the real blocker. "Not worth it yet" is not a reason. Say what is actually missing (no automatic grader, no credential, no adapter) so the user can decide.
  • Never narrate the harness. Hooks, injected context, checklists and memory prompts are machinery aimed at you, not content for the user. Act on them silently. If acting on one produced something real, such as a commit or a file declined, say that in one line as your own decision.

Cost disciplineharnesscore

Every request re-sends the whole context, and the top models charge several times more for new tokens.

Source
working-style.md
How it works

Every request re-sends the whole context, and the top models charge several times more for new tokens. These habits cut the most.

  1. Execution runs on the mid-size model. Use the top model for planning, judgement and adjudication only. When a session is on a top model and the next step is mechanical (edits, renames, test runs, sweeps, formatting, running a known script), say so in one line and suggest switching models. For delegated work, never put the top model inside a fan-out.
  2. Suggest a clear at phase boundaries. A phase ends when a plan is approved, a story is merged, a gate has passed or failed, or the topic changes. Say so in one line and suggest saving a handoff note and clearing, so the next phase starts on a short context. Don't suggest it mid-task, and don't clear the context yourself.
  3. Keep tool output narrow. Pipe long shell output through head, tail or grep. Read a file range, not the whole file, when only part is needed. Send a big read or a wide search to a subagent that returns the conclusion.

When one of these would change what the person asked for, say so and let them decide.

Screenshot loopsharnesscore

Applies to any browser or UI loop that repeats "act, screenshot, read".

Source
working-style.md
How it works

Applies to any browser or UI loop that repeats "act, screenshot, read". Every image read stays in context and is re-sent on every later request.

  1. Read text first. After each action, print the page text (trimmed) or the element you need. Take a screenshot only when text can't answer it: layout, a canvas, an unlabelled button, a visual check.
  2. Don't overwrite and re-read blindly. One screenshot per decision, not one per action. After a run of steps, clear or hand off before the context carries dozens of frames.
  3. Gated steps need every box. On a "tick all boxes" slide, tick every box and confirm each shows checked before pressing Next.

Data integrityharnesscore

Files over 50MB: use sampling, head, or line-by-line processing.

Source
working-style.md
How it works
  • Files over 50MB: use sampling, head, or line-by-line processing. Never read them whole. Check size with ls -lh before reading unknown data files.
  • Before any bulk move or delete, audit first and categorize each item as keep, archive or move. Never batch-delete without verifying import references first.
  • When asked "what is X?" about data or metrics, query the data directly, not the script. Show samples if unclear. Only debug scripts if they crash or produce wrong numbers.
  • Before reporting a file as absent, check the search command exited 0 and list the obvious folder by name. A failed search (for example a shell glob error) is not a negative result.
  • A count piped from a remote listing reads 0 when the listing fails (network, auth). Write the listing to a file, check its exit status, and only then count. Never delete, move or report "empty" on a count whose command did not exit 0.

File organizationharnesscore

If the project has an ARCHITECTURE.md, read it for file placement rules.

Source
working-style.md
How it works
  • If the project has an ARCHITECTURE.md, read it for file placement rules.
  • No loose files in doc directories. Use proper subfolders.
  • No junk docs: no completion, success, validation or summary reports unless explicitly asked.

When moving or reorganizing files, update these in the same operation, as one atomic change:

  1. INDEX.md, with every path that changed.
  2. README.md, including the structure section and any file references.
  3. Any other navigation or index file in the affected directory.
  4. Config files that hardcode a snapshot of the folder layout. They drift silently when folders move, so regenerate them in the same commit.

.env filesharnesscore

The .env file must be source-compatible (bash/zsh).

Source
working-style.md
How it works

The .env file must be source-compatible (bash/zsh). Every non-comment, non-blank line is KEY=value or KEY="quoted value". Never add raw CLI output, colon-separated values, or prose without a # prefix.

When adding a key: use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE=value with no spaces around =, put a # comment above it explaining its purpose, comment out reference-only data, and check the key doesn't already exist.

agent-boardharnessmulti-agent

Keeps an eye on your other herdr agent tabs: shows their state and context size, pops a message when one finishes or gets stuck, and adds /tabs. Needs herdr and Claude Code 2.1.287 or newer; does nothing outside herdr.

Events
command.run, session.start
Commands
/tabs
Settings
AGENT_BOARD_COMPACT=1 (off by default)
Licence
MIT
Runs code
Yes: mod hooks (TypeScript)
Sends text off the machine
No
Source
plugins/agent-board
How it works

When you have four agent tabs open, you stop noticing which one is waiting for you. A short message appears in your current tab the moment another tab goes from working to done or blocked.

  • /tabs lists every other agent tab: its state (working, idle, done, blocked), which tool it runs (claude, codex and so on), its name, and how many tokens of context it holds when that is known.
  • A message appears for about 15 seconds when another tab goes from working to done or blocked.
  • The plugin checks herdr every 30 seconds, so a message can arrive up to half a minute late.
  • The tabs are also kept as one line of text that other mods can show; for example cache-clock draws it above the prompt. Without such a mod you still get the messages and /tabs.

### Where context sizes come from

  • Codex tabs: read from Codex's own session files in ~/.codex/sessions. This needs python3; if it is missing, the size is left out.
  • Claude tabs: a tab can publish its size by writing { "tokens": 123000, "window": 200000 } to /tmp/agent-board-ctx/<pane id>.json, with each character other than a letter, digit, dot or dash in the pane id replaced by _. The context-guard mod does this. Files older than an hour are ignored.
  • Other tools: shown without a size.

### Optional: compact idle Codex tabs (off by default)

If you set AGENT_BOARD_COMPACT=1, a Codex tab that has been idle or done for 10 minutes with more than 150,000 tokens of context is sent /compact once, and you get a message saying so. To turn it on for every Claude Code session, add "env": { "AGENT_BOARD_COMPACT": "1" } to your Claude Code settings file. This types into another tab on your behalf, which is why it is off until you ask.

big-read-guardharnesscore

Refuses whole-file Reads of text files over 50 KB. Needs awk.

Events
session.start, tool.call
Licence
MIT
Runs code
Yes: mod hooks (TypeScript)
Sends text off the machine

Source
plugins/big-read-guard
How it works

Refuses a whole-file Read of a text file over 50 KB and tells Claude to grep the file or read a range with offset and limit, so a big file does not ride along in every later request. A Read that names both offset and limit always goes through. To read a big file on purpose, the refusal message gives the exact offset: 1, limit: <lines> to use. Skipped file endings: .png .jpg .jpeg .gif .webp .pdf .ipynb, plus any you list.

An A/B run of 6 big-file tasks (3 runs each way, Sonnet) found no token difference, because Claude almost never read a whole big file when asked a pointed question; the guard never fired in those runs. It is a safety net, not a measured saving.

Source
plugins/cache-clock
How it works

Claude Code keeps the start of a conversation in a prompt cache so repeat requests are cheaper. When the cache goes cold the next request re-sends everything at full price. This mod draws a countdown bar above the prompt, turns it yellow with 10 minutes left, and shows a toast at 5 minutes. A running turn refreshes the cache on every request, so the countdown only counts down between turns. A button compacts the conversation, which starts a new short prefix and resets the clock. Under the bar one line shows notes from the unattended and layman plugins.

The cache lifetime defaults to 60 minutes (a subscription). On API billing or in usage overage it is 5 minutes: set the environment variable CACHE_CLOCK_TTL_MINUTES=5 to match.

There is a similar plugin, cache-tax, in this marketplace. They overlap; install the one you prefer.

collision-guardharnesscore

Asks before Claude edits a file that something else changed in the last 30 minutes. Needs nothing; reads the unattended plugin's state if present.

Events
session.start, tool.call
Licence
MIT
Runs code
Yes: mod hooks (TypeScript)
Sends text off the machine
No
Source
plugins/collision-guard
How it works

When Claude is about to use Edit, Write or NotebookEdit on a file, the mod checks the file's modified time. If the file changed within the last 30 minutes and this session did not make that change, it asks "Edit it anyway?" with Proceed or Cancel. Cancel refuses the edit and tells Claude why. A file this session wrote itself is only flagged again if its modified time later differs from what this session left. If the check itself fails, the edit goes ahead as normal.

context-guardharnesscore

Warns when the conversation context gets large; opt-in auto-compact of idle sessions. Needs nothing.

Sends text off the machine
No. Opt-in auto-compact is an ordinary model call.
Source
plugins/context-guard
How it works

When the context passes 150K tokens it shows a toast suggesting you save your place and clear, or run /compact, before the next task. It warns again every further 100K tokens. A compaction or /clear that shrinks the context re-arms the warning. Headless runs (claude -p) are never warned.

Optional, off by default: with the environment variable CONTEXT_GUARD_AUTO_COMPACT=1, a session that is idle for 10 minutes with a context over 150K tokens compacts itself. Compacting replaces the conversation history with a summary and spends model tokens, which is why it is opt-in.

disk-sweepharnesscore

macOS only. Warns when your Mac is low on disk space and, with /disk, lists old Claude Code leftovers you can tick and delete. Starts in dry-run mode: it deletes nothing until you turn dryRun off and list a folder in deleteRoots.

Events
command.run, session.start, ui.render
Commands
/disk
Settings
dryRun, deleteRoots, alsoSweep
Licence
MIT
Runs code
Yes: mod hooks (TypeScript)
Sends text off the machine
No
Source
plugins/disk-sweep
How it works

Warns when your Mac is running low on disk space and, when you type /disk, lists old Claude Code leftovers you can tick and delete. Claude Code keeps old plugin versions, conversation transcripts, file backups and debug logs in its config folder, and they pile up over months.

  • Below 30 GB free, a line like 25.0G free · /disk shows in the status area, plus one pop-up note per day.
  • /disk scans and lists what could be removed. /disk --days 30 changes how old a transcript must be to be listed (default 14 days).
  • A panel appears above the prompt. Press Tick on the rows you want, or Tick all safe. Remove ticked asks you to press again; the second press rescans, then acts only on what is still there. Dismiss closes the panel.

### It deletes nothing until you set it up

The plugin starts in dry-run mode. Two options, both in the plugin's configuration, gate deletion:

  • dryRun (default on): Remove ticked only reports and logs what it would delete.
  • deleteRoots (default empty): comma-separated Claude config folders under your home folder, ~ allowed, for example ~/.claude. Only paths under these folders are ever deleted; anything else is skipped and logged. With an empty list nothing is deleted, even with dryRun off. The plugin never guesses a folder for you.
  • alsoSweep (default empty): more config folders to scan along with this session's, for example ~/.claude-work. Scanning only lists; deleting still needs deleteRoots.

Every action goes to ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/disk-sweep.log: what it would remove, what it is removing, what it removed or failed on, and what it skipped. If the log cannot be written, nothing is deleted.

### What it can list

| Kind | What | Rule | |---|---|---| | safe | Old plugin versions in plugins/cache/ | Not the installed version, a newer version is installed, and it is 1 day past Claude's own "orphaned" mark or 7 days untouched | | safe | Leftover plugin download folders (temp_git_*, temp_subdir_*) | Older than 1 day | | safe | file-history/ files | Older than 30 days | | safe | debug/ files | Older than 7 days | | look | Conversation transcripts in projects/ | Older than the cutoff, one row per project. Deleted transcripts can no longer be resumed. |

Anything else in your Claude folder (memory, plans, skills, settings, marketplaces) is never listed.

dispatch-routerharnessmulti-agent

Asks a TypeSafe model which CLI and model should take each agent task and refuses unrouted launches. Needs a TypeSafe API key; without one it does nothing. Sends task text to api.typesafe.ai.

Licence
MIT
Runs code
Yes: mod hooks (TypeScript)
Sends text off the machine
Yes: task text (first 4,000 characters) to api.typesafe.ai with your key.
Source
plugins/dispatch-router
How it works

Claude gets a tool, mcp__dispatch-router__route. Before starting an agent (a terminal tab, an Agent tool call, optionally a cloud session), Claude passes the task text. A TypeSafe model picks the cheapest runner that fits (a Claude model tier, Codex, or agy) and the tool returns the exact launch command and the files the brief must point at.

After that the plugin checks launches. A claude, codex or agy command (also when typed into a pane with herdr pane run or send-keys), or an Agent tool call, is refused unless a routed decision matches it: the same CLI, the same model, launched within 30 minutes. A decision is used once. Forks, claude plugin ..., agy models and similar non-session commands pass.

With no key, it does nothing and shows one notice at session start.

image-shrinkerharnesscore

Shrinks big images before Claude reads them. macOS only: needs sips.

Events
tool.call
Licence
MIT
Runs code
Yes: mod hooks (TypeScript)
Sends text off the machine
No
Source
plugins/image-shrinker
How it works

Every image Claude reads stays in the conversation and is sent again with every later message. A few full-size screenshots can fill Claude's memory for the rest of the session. Shrinking them keeps long sessions going longer.

Example: Claude saves a screenshot of your app to a file after every step and reads each file back. Without this mod, each 2400 pixel wide frame piles up. With it, Claude sees a 1200 pixel wide copy and is told "multiply positions by 2.00" to get back to the original image's pixels. ("Coordinates" are the two numbers, across and down, that say where something is in a picture.) Turning those into clicks on a page depends on the screen: on a Retina screen the image has two pixels for every page pixel, so the number is not a click position by itself.

plugins/input-router
How it works

When Claude reads a long file, the whole text lands in the chat and stays there for the rest of the session. Say you ask "what did we decide about refunds?" and Claude opens a 15,000-token call transcript. With this mod on, Haiku reads the transcript, keeps the refund decision with its time stamp, owner and ticket number, and Claude gets about 300 tokens of notes and the file's path. If the notes are not enough, Claude reads the parts it needs, or the whole file again.

This leaves more room in the chat before it fills up and compacts. Whether it saves money depends on how you work; see "How much it saves" below.

plugins/next-steps-autopilot
How it works

After most replies, a "What next?" button appears above the prompt box. Press it and Claude Code shows up to three prompts you might type next. You pick one, check it and press Enter. Nothing is sent for you unless you turn on /auto.

  • After a reply of 80 characters or more (configurable), "What next?" appears. Press 1 (with an empty prompt box) or click it.
  • Press 1, 2 or 3 (with an empty prompt box) to put that suggestion in the box. Edit it, then press Enter. 0 dismisses the suggestions. Tab takes the greyed-out first suggestion.

### Auto mode

Off at the start of every session.

  • /auto or /auto on: after each reply, suggestions are asked for at once and suggestion 1 is sent after the countdown (10 seconds unless you changed the "Auto mode countdown" option).
  • /auto 5: turn it on with a 5 second countdown for this session. Any whole number up to 999 works.
  • /auto 0 or /auto instant: send at once, no countdown. The next plain /auto goes back to a countdown.
  • /auto off: stop.
  • Press 0 or start typing to stop a countdown. A prompt you send yourself resets the run.
  • It stops after 10 sends in a row until you send something yourself.
  • A suggestion that mentions merge, push, delete, deploy, force, reset, drop, rm, publish or release is never sent by itself; it stays on screen for you to press.

plugins/park
How it works

/park saves your work in the current Claude Code tab and writes a short note for your next session. /unpark reads that note and picks up where you stopped.

  • /park saves this tab and writes the next-session note. The note has ten headings: Goal, Done, Open, First step, Decisions and why, Ruled out, Files read and edited, Skills and tools used, Sources and links, Verify command.
  • When the note is done, a ## Facts (from code, not from the model) block is added: the files edited this session, the git status --short lines (left out outside a git repo) and your last five prompts word for word.
  • You are then asked "Note saved. Continue in a fresh chat?". "Clear and continue" runs /clear and the new chat starts with "Read .park/<note> and follow it." "Stay here", Escape, or any error leaves your chat as it was.
  • /unpark reads the newest note and follows it. At session start, a short message tells you if a note from the last 3 days exists.
  • With herdr (see below), /park also asks every other idle agent tab to save first, and /park close closes the tabs that saved.

Notes go to the .park/ folder of the project, as .park/park-<topic>.md. You may want to add .park/ to your .gitignore.

How it works

Watches subreddits you pick and shows the posts that could improve how you use Claude Code, in a side pane with links. By default it watches r/ClaudeCode posts with the "Built with Claude" flair. Claude's small model (Haiku) reads each new post once and keeps only the ones that give you something specific to try.

  • /reddit on turns it on and scans the latest posts now. It then checks again every hour while Claude Code is open.
  • /reddit off turns it off. A check already under way stops before its next step; a request already sent to Haiku may still finish.
  • /reddit scan checks for new posts now (only while watching is on).
  • /reddit opens the side pane.
  • /reddit add <subreddit> [flair] watches another subreddit, for example /reddit add ClaudeAI Built with Claude. [flair] is an optional label, typed without the brackets, that limits the watch to posts with it.
  • /reddit remove <subreddit> stops watching one.
  • /reddit list shows what is watched, whether it is on, and how many tokens Haiku has used.
  • /reddit clear empties the list of posts shown in the pane.
  • /reddit reset forgets which posts were already read and starts over; if watching is on, it re-reads them all, which costs tokens.

plugins/strict-guard
How it works

Checks every rm, git reset --hard, git clean, force push and migration command in a Bash call. It allows the harmless ones (a temporary folder, a build leftover, nothing discarded, no commits dropped) and refuses the rest. It never runs the guarded command and never asks you. A refusal goes back to Claude with the reason and a request to ask you instead.

This is a text check on the command line, not a sandbox: it cannot see what a shell alias, a function, a variable used as a command name, a script it calls, or another interpreter (python -c, su -c, busybox rm) would delete, so treat it as a safety net for mistakes, not a security boundary.

Stops a Claude Code session from asking you questions when nobody is at the keyboard. Type /unattended, or launch with CLAUDE_UNATTENDED=1. Needs Claude Code 2.1.287 or newer.

plugins/unattended
How it works

Stops a session from asking you questions when nobody is at the keyboard. When it is on, Claude's question prompts and plan mode are refused with a note telling Claude to pick the most sensible option itself and carry on.

Example: you ask Claude to clean up a folder and go for lunch. Claude would normally stop and ask which of two naming styles to use. With this mod on, it picks one, tells you which and why in its reply, and keeps going.

  • /unattended flips the mode on or off. /unattended on and /unattended off set it.
  • To start a session already on, launch with CLAUDE_UNATTENDED=1, for example CLAUDE_UNATTENDED=1 claude.
  • Off by default; applies to the current session only.

### Route mode, for worker agents

A worker agent in a tuios window should not guess: the orchestrator has context it lacks. In route mode a refused question goes into the worker's task file instead of being dropped.

  • /unattended route, or launch with CLAUDE_UNATTENDED=route and CLAUDE_TASK_FILE=<path to the task file>.
  • When Claude asks a question, the mod appends a STATUS: blocked line to the task file, then one QUESTION: line per question with the options Claude was going to offer. Claude is told to carry on with any part of the task that does not depend on the answer, or stop if nothing does.
  • tuios-worker-watch.sh in multi-agent-kit already wakes the orchestrator on a new STATUS: blocked line. The orchestrator answers with tuios-send-verified.sh, or asks you when the decision is yours.
  • If CLAUDE_TASK_FILE is unset, or the file cannot be written, the mod falls back to on mode (Claude picks and carries on) and says why in the refusal, so a worker is never left stuck.
  • Plan mode is refused in route mode just as in on mode.

Example task file after a refused question:

STATUS: blocked
QUESTION: Which naming style should the new files use? Options: kebab-case | snake_case

How it works

When a session starts, it lists the forks in the GitHub account you name and removes the stale ones. A fork is stale only if all of these hold:

  • it belongs to the account you set;
  • it was created at least the number of days you set (default 90);
  • it has a single branch and no commits that are missing from its parent repository;
  • it is not on your keep list;
  • the account is the one gh is signed in as (an organisation name is refused).

Until you turn on "Delete for real", it only writes what it would delete to the log. With no account set, it does nothing and makes no call to GitHub.

MIT
Source
SKILL.md
How it works

# Splitting work between agents

An agent starts with none of your context and returns one summary. Hand it work it can finish and you can check, and keep your own context for decisions.

## When to hand work off

Hand off work that needs many files read, many edits, or a test run: the agent spends its own context on it and you receive a short result. Do small things yourself: a one-line fix or a config tweak costs less than writing the brief.

Don't read files in your own session just to describe them to an agent. Name the task and where to look; it reads what it needs.

## Where the agents run

  • Ask every time. Before the first hand-off of a task, ask the user whether to run the agents as tuios windows or as subagents inside this session. Never pick for them, even when an earlier task used tuios.
  • tuios view in the caller's space. When the user picks tuios, show the tuios view in the herdr space this session runs in. In the Herdr app (HC_TERMINAL_ID set), use herdr-core run. With the herdr CLI, reuse or create the agents (tuios) tab in the current workspace. If neither is running, ask the user where to show it. Never open a separate Terminal window.
  • The launch steps (session, one worktree per window, auto mode, attach, short prompt) are in this plugin's README under "Running agents in tuios".

## The brief

  • One task per agent. If the brief has an "and" joining two outcomes, make two briefs.
  • Own files. Say which files or folders the agent may change. Two agents never edit the same file.
  • A named check. Give the command or condition that proves the work is done (a test, a build, a diff to compare). An agent without one reports "done" on its own judgment.
  • Own worktree when parallel. Agents running at the same time each get their own git worktree and branch, so they cannot overwrite each other or leave your tree half-edited.
  • Brief in a file. Write the task to a file and point the agent at it. A file can be re-read, reviewed and reused after a restart; a long pasted prompt cannot.
  • Result in a file. Ask the agent to write its report to a named path (what it changed, what the check printed, what it could not do), so you read the result without replaying the session. A last line such as STATUS: done or STATUS: blocked lets a script or hook see the outcome.

## After it finishes

Run the named check yourself before accepting the result. Read the report for what the agent skipped or could not do. Merge one branch at a time and re-run the check after each merge, so a failure points at one change.

## Other CLIs

Another CLI (Codex, agy, and so on) does not load this project's CLAUDE.md or hooks. Point its brief at the rule files it needs.

repo-health:repo-healthharnesscore

Read-only health check of a git repo and its GitHub remote. Reports open PRs, local and remote branches (merged, unpushed, stale), worktrees with their disk size, and stashes, then sorts them into safe to delete, needs a look, and keep. Use when the user asks about open PRs, how many branches exist, stale or merged branches, branch cleanup, worktree clutter, or a GitHub/repo health check. Deletes nothing without approval.

Part of
repo-health
Licence
MIT
Source
SKILL.md
How it works

# Repo health

## 1. Run the report

From the repo root:

bash ~/.claude/skills/repo-health/repo-health.sh

Needs gh authenticated, jq, and the gh-poi extension (gh extension install seachicken/gh-poi).

The script is read-only apart from git fetch --prune.

## 2. Read the columns correctly

  • files differing from main: of the files the branch changed since it forked, how many still differ from main. 0 means its work is in main, including after a squash merge (git cherry and git branch --merged both miss squash merges). It over-counts when main edited those files later, so a MERGED PR with a small non-zero count is usually fine, while a MERGED PR with a large count means work was added after the merge; inspect before deleting. ? means no shared history with main (e.g. an old master).
  • PR is the newest PR for that branch name. no PR plus unique commits means work that exists nowhere else.
  • [gone] in upstream means GitHub deleted the remote after merge.

## 3. Classify

| Bucket | Rule | |---|---| | Safe to delete | listed by gh poi, or PR MERGED/CLOSED with 0 commits not in main | | Needs a look | unique commits and no open PR; never pushed; dirty worktree; PR open but far behind main; old stashes | | Keep | open PR, checked out in a clean active worktree, main |

Present the three lists as tables, plus any headline problems (checkout sitting on a merged branch, main behind origin, missing worktree directories).

## 4. Cleanup only on approval

Never delete in the same turn as the report unless the user already said to. Before deleting, write name sha for every branch to a file in the scratchpad so any of them can be restored with git branch <name> <sha>.

  • Local merged branches: gh poi (it skips worktrees and the current branch).
  • Local squash-merged with 0 unique: git branch -D <name>.
  • Remote: git push origin --delete <name>. This is visible to others; confirm the list first.
  • Worktrees: git worktree remove <path> only when clean and its branch has 0 unique commits. Check with ListAgents or ask first, because a peer session may be working in it.
  • Stashes: show git stash show -p stash@{n} before any drop. Never drop without approval.

web-access:web-accessharnesscore

Use whenever a task needs something from the live web — search the web or the news, read a URL, map or crawl a site, pull structured fields from a page, or get data from a platform (X, LinkedIn, Reddit, TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, Amazon, app stores, Google Maps, papers). Picks the right tool for the job, starts free, and lets treg fall back to the next vendor when one fails. No local scrapers, browsers or cookies.

Part of
web-access
Licence
MIT
Source
SKILL.md
How it works

# Web access

One treg key reads the web: free search and page fetch first, and the rest of the catalog behind them for the pages and platforms a free fetch can't reach. Nothing runs on this machine: no browser, no cookies, no burner accounts. treg calls the vendor and, on a routed job, tries the next one when a vendor comes back empty or blocked.

Runs on treg. If it isn't set up (treg --version fails), read https://treg.to/llms.txt and follow it to install and sign in, then come back here.

## Pick the job

Know the URL?             → read it (free first)
Need to find pages?       → search (free) → read the 3–5 best results
A platform object?        → never scrape its HTML: use the platform's job
  (post, profile, video,     structured fields, fewer tokens, survives redesigns
   product, review, place)
A whole site?             → map it → read only the pages that matter
Need typed fields?        → structured extract with a JSON schema or an instruction
Need it recent or dated?  → news search, not web search

## Free first

Web search and page reads are free through TinyFish:

  • treg call treg.web.search --data '{"q":"…"}' --header 'X-Treg-Route-Prefer: tinyfish'
  • treg call treg.web.extract --data '{"url":"…"}' --header 'X-Treg-Route-Prefer: tinyfish'

Both are routed: when TinyFish comes back empty or blocked, treg tries the next vendor (Crawl4AI, AnyAPI, …). You pay the vendor that answered plus any vendor before it that bills a miss (treg catalog get says how many do); X-Treg-Route-Max-Cost caps the walk. To read up to ten URLs in one free call, call tinyfish.web.fetch directly with {"urls":[…]}; it does not fall back.

Platform data (social, stores, reviews, maps) is not free: cents or fractions of a cent a call. Say so before a batch.

## Jobs

Search the catalog for the words in the second column. The vendors are examples of who answers today; take whatever the catalog ranks best now.

| You want | Search the catalog for | Example vendors | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Web results | treg.web.search | TinyFish, Exa, Perplexity, Keenable | free with the TinyFish header | | A page as markdown | treg.web.extract | TinyFish, Crawl4AI, AnyAPI | free first; blocked pages fall back | | Typed fields from a page | treg.web.extract.structured | | send url plus a schema and/or instruction | | Every URL on a site | treg.web.map | AnyAPI, Firecrawl, Tavily | add q to rank URLs for a topic | | Many pages of a site | "crawl a website" | Firecrawl, Crawl4AI, Olostep | map first when you need only some pages | | Recent news | treg.web.search.news | Serper, DataForSEO, Exa | dated results | | Papers | "search research publications" | TinyFish, Exa, Serper | | | X, LinkedIn, Reddit, TikTok, Instagram, Threads, Facebook | "x search posts", "linkedin company posts", "reddit subreddit posts", "tiktok video comments", … | TikHub, ScrapeCreators, HarvestAPI, AnyAPI | profiles, posts, comments, reactions as fields | | YouTube, Bilibili | "youtube video comments", "youtube search videos" | Crawl4AI, TikHub, ScrapeCreators | | | Douyin, Weibo | "douyin search videos" | TikHub, JustOneAPI | | | Stores | "amazon product detail", "amazon search products", "walmart search", "ebay search" | JustOneAPI, SerpAPI, Crawl4AI | price, rating, reviews as fields | | Reviews | "app store reviews", "google play app", "trustpilot reviews", "glassdoor reviews", "google maps reviews" | Crawl4AI, Bright Data, LiteScrape | | | Places | "google maps search", "local results" | DataForSEO, SerpAPI | | | Google results as Google shows them | "google serp organic" | DataForSEO, Serper | ranks, snippets, features |

## Finding the endpoint

The catalog changes every week, so never trust a remembered endpoint id.

  1. treg catalog search "<the job in plain words>", not a vendor name.
  2. Prefer a routed treg.* endpoint when there is one: the team's own keys first, then vendors in order, and most misses are free.
  3. treg catalog get <id>: the price, the vendors behind a routed job, and each one's measured hit rate (it found something), not just works (it returned 200), and speed.
  4. One small call first. Read _treg.served_by, _treg.tried and the reported charge, then scale.
  5. Nothing fits: treg catalog request "<what is missing>".

## Steering a routed job

Options ride as headers, never in the body:

| Header | Use it to | | --- | --- | | X-Treg-Route-Prefer: <vendor> | try that vendor first (free TinyFish, or the one that worked last time) | | X-Treg-Route-Exclude: <vendor> | skip a vendor that gave you bad answers | | X-Treg-Route-Max-Cost: <usd> | cap one call; uncapped, a miss can walk up to $1 of vendors | | X-Treg-Route-Waterfall: 0 | stop at the first miss when only one vendor's answer will do |

Batches: always send a Max-Cost.

## Habits that save money and tokens

  • Read pages as markdown, and cut navigation and footers before they reach the context.
  • A platform job returns fields; a scraped page of the same thing costs several times the tokens.
  • Search, then read only the results you need. Never read a whole site to answer one question.
  • Keep the source URL next to every fact you hand back.

## Recipes

  • Research a company: web search → read its site, pricing and docs pages → news search for the last 90 days → its LinkedIn company profile.
  • Read a docs site into context: map the site with q set to the topic → read the top pages.
  • Watch a page for changes: read it, keep a hash of the text, read it again next run and report the diff. Schedule it with the user's agent (Claude Code /schedule or /loop, cron for others).
  • Social listening: search posts on X, Reddit and LinkedIn → read the comments on the best ones → summarise by theme with links.
  • Compare a product across stores: search it on each store → product detail for the matches → one table of price, rating and review count.
  • Collect reviews: app store and Google Play for apps, Trustpilot and Glassdoor for companies, Google Maps for places → quote the patterns, with counts.
  • Videos into notes: YouTube search → video detail and comments → summarise.

## Check the setup

treg --version && treg balance
treg call treg.web.search --data '{"q":"treg web access"}' --header 'X-Treg-Route-Prefer: tinyfish'

A result with _treg.served_by and no charge means free search works. Something wrong: treg feedback "<what happened>" reaches the team.

## Lines not to cross

Public data only. Never log in as the user, ask for their cookies or get round a paywall. Don't bulk collect personal data about private individuals. When a vendor refuses a page, take the fallback or tell the user; don't hammer it.
